newsitem.title: BULGARIA: PARTY CRITICS SEEKS CHALLENGER TO BULGARIA PREMIER.
newsitem.headline: PARTY CRITICS SEEKS CHALLENGER TO BULGARIA PREMIER.

text.p: Reformists in the Bulgarian Socialist Party, wrong-footed by the surprise resignation of Prime Minister Zhan Videnov, met through the night at a party congress but have not yet agreed on a candidate to replace him.
Videnov stunned delegates by announcing at Saturday's opening session that he felt he lacked the necessary support to continue as premier and party leader.

"This decision should have been taken 40 days ago when it became evident that there was no confidence in the government," said foreign minister Georgi Pirinski, who resigned last month after a party confidence vote gave Videnov only narrow backing.

Pirinski told the congress on Sunday he had quit because the confidence vote had shown Videnov did not enjoy the public support he needed to implement a tough monetary regime proposed by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) as a last-ditch attempt to halt economic collapse.
Delegates painted a bleak picture of the country's crisis and called for a genuine commitment to reform and concrete measures to fight corruption.
Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev, another potential rival to Videnov, said the premier had not accepted enough responsibility for the disastrous state of the country.
"I insist on a change of policy and a change in the style of government," he said.
"The fight against corruption should be a main aim for this congress," he said, citing crooked insurance companies who cooperated with officials of his ministry.

Party reformists met into the early hours on the longest night of the year but said they had not so far been able to agree on one candidate to replace Videnov, whose supporters are expected to ask him to stand again.
Sunday's newspapers dismissed the resignation as a ploy by the 37-year-old premier to show he had popular support and editorials ironically begged him not to quit.
"Zhan, please don't go, there's no need for you to go now, Bulgaria's finished already," said Troud daily. Standard said there would no longer be anything to put in the newspaper.

The communist-style congress, which must also name a new cabinet, is expected to continue into Monday. The main hall in the National Palace of Culture is decorated with Christmas trees, Bulgarian flags and red party flags for the event.

Videnov became prime minister after parliamentary elections in December 1994. Criticism of his government, which is half way through its four year term, became more vocal after the Socialists' defeat in last month's presidential election.
Leading members of the Bulgarian Communist Party renamed themselves Socialists after the end of one-party rule in 1989.
The government's failure to meet reform targets including closing or restructuring loss-making state enterprises has led to the suspension of funding from the World Bank and IMF.

The government has not yet finalised the 1997 budget. Videnov has accepted an IMF proposal for a currency board fixed exchange rate mechanism, expected to be set up early next year to restore confidence and halt the slide in the lev.
Deputy Prime Minister Roumen Gechev told the congress the lev should be pegged to the mark in the currency board, which matches levs in circulation to central bank reserves.
The dollar is psychologically important to Bulgarians who use it as a refuge for their savings, but Germany is Bulgaria's main foreign trade partner.
An IMF technical mission left on Friday and negotiators are due back in the New Year to finalise the currency board.
